CHAPTER XIII.


Their intended excursion to Whitwell turned out very different from
what Elinor had expected. She was prepared to be wet through, fatigued,
and frightened; but the event was still more unfortunate, for they did
not go at all.

By ten o’clock the whole party was assembled at the park, where they
were to breakfast. The morning was rather favourable, though it had
rained all night, as the clouds were then dispersing across the sky,
and the sun frequently appeared. They were all in high spirits and good
humour, eager to be happy, and determined to submit to the greatest
inconveniences and hardships rather than be otherwise.

While they were at breakfast the letters were brought in. Among the
rest there was one for Colonel Brandon;—he took it, looked at the
direction, changed colour, and immediately left the room.

“What is the matter with Brandon?” said Sir John.

Nobody could tell.

“I hope he has had no bad news,” said Lady Middleton. “It must be
something extraordinary that could make Colonel Brandon leave my
breakfast table so suddenly.”

In about five minutes he returned.

“No bad news, Colonel, I hope;” said Mrs. Jennings, as soon as he
entered the room.

“None at all, ma’am, I thank you.”

“Was it from Avignon? I hope it is not to say that your sister is
worse.”

“No, ma’am. It came from town, and is merely a letter of business.”

“But how came the hand to discompose you so much, if it was only a
letter of business? Come, come, this won’t do, Colonel; so let us hear
the truth of it.”

“My dear madam,” said Lady Middleton, “recollect what you are saying.”

“Perhaps it is to tell you that your cousin Fanny is married?” said
Mrs. Jennings, without attending to her daughter’s reproof.

“No, indeed, it is not.”

“Well, then, I know who it is from, Colonel. And I hope she is well.”

“Whom do you mean, ma’am?” said he, colouring a little.

“Oh! you know who I mean.”

“I am particularly sorry, ma’am,” said he, addressing Lady Middleton,
“that I should receive this letter today, for it is on business which
requires my immediate attendance in town.”

“In town!” cried Mrs. Jennings. “What can you have to do in town at
this time of year?”

“My own loss is great,” he continued, “in being obliged to leave so
agreeable a party; but I am the more concerned, as I fear my presence
is necessary to gain your admittance at Whitwell.”

What a blow upon them all was this!

“But if you write a note to the housekeeper, Mr. Brandon,” said
Marianne, eagerly, “will it not be sufficient?”

He shook his head.

“We must go,” said Sir John.—“It shall not be put off when we are so
near it. You cannot go to town till tomorrow, Brandon, that is all.”

“I wish it could be so easily settled. But it is not in my power to
delay my journey for one day!”

“If you would but let us know what your business is,” said Mrs.
Jennings, “we might see whether it could be put off or not.”

“You would not be six hours later,” said Willoughby, “if you were to
defer your journey till our return.”

“I cannot afford to lose _one_ hour.”

Elinor then heard Willoughby say, in a low voice to Marianne, “There
are some people who cannot bear a party of pleasure. Brandon is one of
them. He was afraid of catching cold I dare say, and invented this
trick for getting out of it. I would lay fifty guineas the letter was
of his own writing.”

“I have no doubt of it,” replied Marianne.

“There is no persuading you to change your mind, Brandon, I know of
old,” said Sir John, “when once you are determined on anything. But,
however, I hope you will think better of it. Consider, here are the two
Miss Careys come over from Newton, the three Miss Dashwoods walked up
from the cottage, and Mr. Willoughby got up two hours before his usual
time, on purpose to go to Whitwell.”

Colonel Brandon again repeated his sorrow at being the cause of
disappointing the party; but at the same time declared it to be
unavoidable.

“Well, then, when will you come back again?”

“I hope we shall see you at Barton,” added her ladyship, “as soon as
you can conveniently leave town; and we must put off the party to
Whitwell till you return.”

“You are very obliging. But it is so uncertain, when I may have it in
my power to return, that I dare not engage for it at all.”

“Oh! he must and shall come back,” cried Sir John. “If he is not here
by the end of the week, I shall go after him.”

“Ay, so do, Sir John,” cried Mrs. Jennings, “and then perhaps you may
find out what his business is.”

“I do not want to pry into other men’s concerns. I suppose it is
something he is ashamed of.”

Colonel Brandon’s horses were announced.

“You do not go to town on horseback, do you?” added Sir John.

“No. Only to Honiton. I shall then go post.”

“Well, as you are resolved to go, I wish you a good journey. But you
had better change your mind.”

“I assure you it is not in my power.”

He then took leave of the whole party.

“Is there no chance of my seeing you and your sisters in town this
winter, Miss Dashwood?”

“I am afraid, none at all.”

“Then I must bid you farewell for a longer time than I should wish to
do.”

To Marianne, he merely bowed and said nothing.

“Come Colonel,” said Mrs. Jennings, “before you go, do let us know what
you are going about.”

He wished her a good morning, and, attended by Sir John, left the room.

The complaints and lamentations which politeness had hitherto
restrained, now burst forth universally; and they all agreed again and
again how provoking it was to be so disappointed.

“I can guess what his business is, however,” said Mrs. Jennings
exultingly.

“Can you, ma’am?” said almost every body.

“Yes; it is about Miss Williams, I am sure.”

“And who is Miss Williams?” asked Marianne.

“What! do not you know who Miss Williams is? I am sure you must have
heard of her before. She is a relation of the Colonel’s, my dear; a
very near relation. We will not say how near, for fear of shocking the
young ladies.” Then, lowering her voice a little, she said to Elinor,
“She is his natural daughter.”

“Indeed!”

“Oh, yes; and as like him as she can stare. I dare say the Colonel will
leave her all his fortune.”

When Sir John returned, he joined most heartily in the general regret
on so unfortunate an event; concluding however by observing, that as
they were all got together, they must do something by way of being
happy; and after some consultation it was agreed, that although
happiness could only be enjoyed at Whitwell, they might procure a
tolerable composure of mind by driving about the country. The carriages
were then ordered; Willoughby’s was first, and Marianne never looked
happier than when she got into it. He drove through the park very fast,
and they were soon out of sight; and nothing more of them was seen till
their return, which did not happen till after the return of all the
rest. They both seemed delighted with their drive; but said only in
general terms that they had kept in the lanes, while the others went on
the downs.

It was settled that there should be a dance in the evening, and that
every body should be extremely merry all day long. Some more of the
Careys came to dinner, and they had the pleasure of sitting down nearly
twenty to table, which Sir John observed with great contentment.
Willoughby took his usual place between the two elder Miss Dashwoods.
Mrs. Jennings sat on Elinor’s right hand; and they had not been long
seated, before she leant behind her and Willoughby, and said to
Marianne, loud enough for them both to hear, “I have found you out in
spite of all your tricks. I know where you spent the morning.”

Marianne coloured, and replied very hastily, “Where, pray?”

“Did not you know,” said Willoughby, “that we had been out in my
curricle?”

“Yes, yes, Mr. Impudence, I know that very well, and I was determined
to find out _where_ you had been to. I hope you like your house, Miss
Marianne. It is a very large one, I know; and when I come to see you, I
hope you will have new-furnished it, for it wanted it very much when I
was there six years ago.”

Marianne turned away in great confusion. Mrs. Jennings laughed
heartily; and Elinor found that in her resolution to know where they
had been, she had actually made her own woman enquire of Mr.
Willoughby’s groom; and that she had by that method been informed that
they had gone to Allenham, and spent a considerable time there in
walking about the garden and going all over the house.

Elinor could hardly believe this to be true, as it seemed very unlikely
that Willoughby should propose, or Marianne consent, to enter the house
while Mrs. Smith was in it, with whom Marianne had not the smallest
acquaintance.

As soon as they left the dining-room, Elinor enquired of her about it;
and great was her surprise when she found that every circumstance
related by Mrs. Jennings was perfectly true. Marianne was quite angry
with her for doubting it.

“Why should you imagine, Elinor, that we did not go there, or that we
did not see the house? Is not it what you have often wished to do
yourself?”

“Yes, Marianne, but I would not go while Mrs. Smith was there, and with
no other companion than Mr. Willoughby.”

“Mr. Willoughby however is the only person who can have a right to show
that house; and as he went in an open carriage, it was impossible to
have any other companion. I never spent a pleasanter morning in my
life.”

“I am afraid,” replied Elinor, “that the pleasantness of an employment
does not always evince its propriety.”

“On the contrary, nothing can be a stronger proof of it, Elinor; for if
there had been any real impropriety in what I did, I should have been
sensible of it at the time, for we always know when we are acting
wrong, and with such a conviction I could have had no pleasure.”

“But, my dear Marianne, as it has already exposed you to some very
impertinent remarks, do you not now begin to doubt the discretion of
your own conduct?”

“If the impertinent remarks of Mrs. Jennings are to be the proof of
impropriety in conduct, we are all offending every moment of our lives.
I value not her censure any more than I should do her commendation. I
am not sensible of having done anything wrong in walking over Mrs.
Smith’s grounds, or in seeing her house. They will one day be Mr.
Willoughby’s, and—”

“If they were one day to be your own, Marianne, you would not be
justified in what you have done.”

She blushed at this hint; but it was even visibly gratifying to her;
and after a ten minutes’ interval of earnest thought, she came to her
sister again, and said with great good humour, “Perhaps, Elinor, it
_was_ rather ill-judged in me to go to Allenham; but Mr. Willoughby
wanted particularly to show me the place; and it is a charming house, I
assure you.—There is one remarkably pretty sitting room up stairs; of a
nice comfortable size for constant use, and with modern furniture it
would be delightful. It is a corner room, and has windows on two sides.
On one side you look across the bowling-green, behind the house, to a
beautiful hanging wood, and on the other you have a view of the church
and village, and, beyond them, of those fine bold hills that we have so
often admired. I did not see it to advantage, for nothing could be more
forlorn than the furniture,—but if it were newly fitted up—a couple of
hundred pounds, Willoughby says, would make it one of the pleasantest
summer-rooms in England.”

Could Elinor have listened to her without interruption from the others,
she would have described every room in the house with equal delight.

The planned outing to Whitwell turned out far differently than Elinor had anticipated. She had braced herself for damp clothes, exhaustion, and perhaps even a touch of fear—but what actually happened was worse: they didn’t go at all. By ten o’clock, the entire party had gathered at the park, ready to enjoy breakfast before setting off. Though rain had fallen through the night, the morning offered some relief—the clouds were breaking apart, and the sun peeked through now and then. Everyone was in high spirits, eager to make the most of the day, determined to endure any discomfort rather than miss this rare opportunity for joy.

As they sat down to eat, the letters arrived. Among them was one addressed to Colonel Brandon. He took it, glanced at the handwriting, paled slightly, and immediately excused himself from the table.

“What’s wrong with Brandon?” Sir John asked, puzzled.
No one could say.
“I hope he hasn’t received bad news,” Lady Middleton murmured.
“It must be something extraordinary,” Sir John added, “to make Colonel Brandon leave my breakfast table so abruptly.”

After a few minutes, Brandon returned.
“No bad news, Colonel?” Mrs. Jennings asked as soon as he stepped back into the room.
“None at all, ma'am, I thank you.”
“Was it from Avignon? I hope your sister isn’t worse?”
“No, ma'am. It came from town—it’s only business.”
“But why did you turn so pale? If it’s just business, why such a reaction?” she pressed. “Come now, Colonel—let us hear the truth.”

“Dear madam,” Lady Middleton interjected gently, “do remember your manners.”

But Mrs. Jennings paid no heed. “Perhaps it’s to tell you that your cousin Fanny is married?” she guessed.
“No indeed,” Brandon replied.
“Well, then, I know who it’s from,” she declared. “And I hope she’s well.”

“Who do you mean, ma'am?” he asked, his cheeks warming slightly.
“Oh! You know exactly who I mean.”

“I am truly sorry,” he said, turning to Lady Middleton, “that I should receive this letter today. It concerns matters that require my immediate presence in London.”

“In London!” Mrs. Jennings exclaimed. “What on earth could you possibly need there at this time of year?”

“My loss is great,” he continued, “in having to leave such a pleasant gathering. But I’m especially regretful, because I fear my absence may prevent you from gaining admittance to Whitwell.”

It was a devastating blow. The disappointment was palpable.

“But if you write a note to the housekeeper,” Marianne suggested eagerly, “wouldn’t that suffice?”

Brandon shook his head.
“We must go,” Sir John insisted. “We’re too close now to give up. You can’t possibly leave until tomorrow, Brandon—that’s all.”

“I wish it were so simple,” Brandon replied. “But I cannot delay my journey by even a single day.”

“If you’d only let us know what your business is,” Mrs. Jennings urged, “we might see if it could be postponed.”

“You wouldn’t be six hours later,” Willoughby said calmly, “if you waited until we returned.”

“I cannot afford to lose *one* hour,” Brandon repeated firmly.

At that moment, Elinor overheard Willoughby whisper to Marianne, “There are some people who simply can’t stand a good time. Brandon is one of them. He probably just wanted to avoid getting cold—and made up this excuse to get out of it. I’d bet fifty guineas that he wrote the letter himself.”

“I have no doubt of it,” Marianne replied without hesitation.

“Brandon,” Sir John said with a sigh, “you’ve always been stubborn when you set your mind to something. But still, think about it—here are the two Miss Careys come all the way from Newton, the three Miss Dashwoods walked up from the cottage, and Mr. Willoughby rose two hours earlier than usual just to join us at Whitwell.”

Brandon once again expressed his sorrow at causing such dismay, but stood firm in his decision.

“And when will you return?” Lady Middleton asked.
“I hope to see you at Barton soon,” she added, “as soon as you can conveniently leave town. We’ll have to postpone our visit to Whitwell until then.”

“You are very kind,” Brandon replied. “But I cannot promise when I might return—it’s uncertain.”

“Oh, he *must* and *shall* come back!” Sir John declared. “If he’s not here by the end of the week, I’ll go after him myself.”

“Do go, Sir John,” Mrs. Jennings chimed in. “Then maybe you’ll discover what his real business is.”

“I don’t want to pry into other men’s affairs,” Sir John said. “I suppose it’s something he’s ashamed of.”

Just then, the announcement came that Colonel Brandon’s horses were ready.
“You’re not riding all the way to town, are you?” Sir John asked.
“No. Only to Honiton. From there, I’ll take the post-chaise.”

“Well, since you’re resolved to go,” Sir John said, “I wish you a safe journey. But you really ought to reconsider.”

“I assure you,” Brandon said, “it’s beyond my control.”

He then bade farewell to everyone. Turning to Elinor, he said, “Is there any chance I might see you and your sisters in town this winter?”
“I’m afraid not,” she replied.
“Then I must bid you farewell for longer than I would like,” he said quietly.

To Marianne, he merely bowed and said nothing.

“Come, Colonel,” Mrs. Jennings called after him, “before you go—do tell us what this urgent matter is.”

He wished her a good morning and, escorted by Sir John, left the room.

Now, with no restraint of politeness, the full weight of their disappointment poured forth. Every person at the table lamented the ruined plan, repeating over and over how unjust it was to be denied such a day.

“I can guess what his business is,” Mrs. Jennings announced triumphantly.
“Can you, ma'am?” several voices asked.
“Yes,” she declared. “It’s about Miss Williams—I’m certain of it.”

“And who is Miss Williams?” Marianne asked.
“What! Don’t you know who Miss Williams is? You must have heard of her. She’s a relation of the Colonel’s—a very close one. We won’t say just how close, for fear of shocking the young ladies.”

She lowered her voice slightly and leaned toward Elinor. “She’s his natural daughter.”

“Indeed!” Elinor murmured.
“Oh, yes,” Mrs. Jennings confirmed. “And as like him as she can stare. I daresay the Colonel will leave her everything.”

When Sir John returned, he joined in the general regret but quickly shifted the mood. “Since we’re all together,” he said, “we must find some way to enjoy ourselves. Let’s not waste the day.” After brief discussion, they decided that while happiness couldn’t be found at Whitwell, they could at least seek comfort in a country drive.

The carriages were summoned. Willoughby’s curricle was first to depart, and Marianne looked more radiant than ever as she climbed inside. He drove swiftly through the park, and soon they vanished from sight. Not until much later did they return—after all the others had already come back.

Both seemed thoroughly delighted with their ride, though they spoke only in vague terms about keeping to the lanes while the others explored the downs.

That evening, a dance was arranged, and everyone vowed to be exceptionally merry. More of the Carey family arrived for dinner, swelling the company to nearly twenty—a number Sir John found immensely satisfying.

Willoughby took his usual seat between the two elder Miss Dashwoods. Mrs. Jennings sat beside Elinor, and not long after they were seated, she leaned behind them and addressed Marianne loudly enough for both sisters to hear:
“I’ve found you out, despite all your tricks. I know exactly where you spent the morning.”

Marianne flushed and replied sharply, “Where, pray?”

“Didn’t you know,” Willoughby said coolly, “that we went out in my curricle?”

“Yes, yes, Mr. Impudence,” Mrs. Jennings snapped. “I know that well enough. But I was determined to learn *where* you went. I hope you’re enjoying your house, Miss Marianne. It’s quite large, I understand. And when I visit you, I hope you’ll have furnished it properly—because it certainly needed it when I was there six years ago.”

Marianne turned away, deeply embarrassed. Mrs. Jennings laughed heartily.

Later, Elinor discovered that Mrs. Jennings had sent her maid to question Willoughby’s groom—and learned that they had gone to Allenham, spending a considerable time walking through the garden and touring the house.

Elinor found this hard to believe. It seemed unlikely that Willoughby would suggest entering the house while Mrs. Smith was still living there—someone Marianne barely knew.

As soon as they left the dining room, Elinor questioned her sister. Her surprise was immense when Marianne confirmed every detail.

“You doubted me?” Marianne said, annoyed.
“Why should I imagine we didn’t go there—or that we didn’t see the house? Isn’t that something you’ve often wanted to do yourself?”

“Yes,” Elinor admitted, “but I wouldn’t go while Mrs. Smith was there—especially with no one but Mr. Willoughby.”

“But Mr. Willoughby is the only one who has the right to show the house,” Marianne argued. “And since he traveled in an open carriage, we couldn perfection had another companion. I never spent a more delightful morning in my life.”

“I’m afraid,” Elinor replied gently, “that pleasure doesn’t always prove propriety.”

“On the contrary,” Marianne insisted, “nothing could better prove it. If I had done anything truly wrong, I would have felt it at the time—we always know when we’re acting improperly. And if I truly believed I was doing something wrong, I could not have enjoyed it.”

“But,” Elinor said, “since it’s already brought you such impertinent remarks, don’t you now question your own judgment?”

“If Mrs. Jennings’ opinions are to define what’s proper,” Marianne retorted, “then we’re all guilty every minute. I care not for her approval—or her disapproval. I feel no guilt for walking through Mrs. Smith’s grounds or seeing her house. One day, they’ll belong to Mr. Willoughby—and—”

“If they were to become yours someday, Marianne,” Elinor interrupted softly, “would you still consider your actions justified?”

Marianne blushed—but there was a flicker of satisfaction in her eyes. After a pause, she returned to her sister, smiling brightly.
“Perhaps,” she said, “it *was* rather unwise of me to go to Allenham. But Mr. Willoughby was eager to show me the place—and it is truly charming. There’s one remarkable sitting room upstairs—just the right size for daily use, and with modern furnishings, it would be perfect. It’s a corner room with windows on two sides. On one side, you look across the bowling green, behind the house, to a lovely hanging wood. On the other, you see the church and village, and beyond them, those magnificent hills we’ve admired so often. I didn’t see it at its best—the furniture was dreadful—but if it were refurnished—say, two hundred pounds, Willoughby says—it could be one of the most delightful summer rooms in England.”

If Elinor had been able to listen without interruption, Marianne would have described every room in the house with equal enthusiasm.
